scope.start: 5b: the Mishnah's definition of a *katan* and R. Zeira's objection (6a opens mid-exchange)

sections.title: Minor's Obligation: When It Starts (Carried or Walking), and Chinukh
sections.gist: Which child must come to the Temple: the shoulders vs. walking standard, and whether one trains a lame or blind child.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Beit Shammai): a *katan* is exempt if he can't ride on his father's shoulders from Jerusalem up to the Temple Mount.
R. Zeira objects: then who brought him as far as Jerusalem?
Abaye: his mother did, since she is obligated in *simchah*. The test only starts in Jerusalem. By Beit Hillel's standard, if he can walk up holding his father's hand, he is obligated.
Rebbi argues for Beit Hillel from Chana: "until the child is weaned" (I Shmuel 1:22). Shmuel could already ride on shoulders, yet Chana didn't bring him.
His father rejects the proof. Chana herself was obligated in *simchah* and still stayed home, so her reason was personal: Shmuel was delicate and couldn't make the trip.
R. Shimon asks about a lame child who can be carried (for Beit Shammai), or a blind child who can be led (for both schools).
The question is only about a child who may heal. A permanently disabled child will be exempt as an adult too, so there is nothing to train him for.
Abaye: *chinukh* follows what an adult in the same condition owes now. Where such an adult is exempt, the minor is exempt too, even if he may recover.

sections.title: Which Has the Higher Minimum: Olat Re'iyah or Shalmei Chagigah?
sections.gist: Which festival offering must cost more, and, underneath that dispute, what the *olah* brought at Sinai was.

children.title: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel: God's Share or the Shared Offering
children.gist: Beit Shammai make the *re'iyah* the costlier offering and Beit Hillel the *chagigah*. Each side has two arguments and answers the other's.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai: *olat re'iyah* at least 2 silver *kesef*, *shalmei chagigah* at least 1 *ma'ah*. Beit Hillel reverse the two.

Beneath the numbers is a question of emphasis. Beit Shammai favor the *olah*, which is God's alone. Beit Hillel favor the *shelamim*, which God and the worshipper share. At stake is how much the human side counts in worship.
Beit Hillel: Shemot 24:5, "*vayizbechu zevachim shelamim*", shows the *chagigah* type existed before *matan Torah*.
Beit Shammai: the same verse says "*vaya'alu olot*", so the *olah* preceded Sinai as well.
So the dispute becomes: what were those Sinai *olot*? Beit Hillel say the *olat tamid* (communal). Beit Shammai say an *olat re'iyah* (individual).
It is striking that both sides treat pre-Sinai practice as binding precedent at all, when events before *matan Torah* usually carry no legal weight.

chart.caption: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel: which offering costs more
rows: The *nesi'im* brought theirs once; learn from what applies in every generation
The *shelamim* has two "eatings": the altar and the owner
Shavuot's are communal; learn an individual's offering from individuals

children.title: The Olah at Sinai: Re'iyah or Tamid?
children.gist: Abaye extends the question to six *tanna'im*, three on each side. The Gemara then tests his alignment and strikes R. Yishmael from it.

children.title: Six Tannaim, Two Camps
children.gist: Abaye divides six tanna'im into two camps: three say the Sinai *olah* was an *olat re'iyah*, three an *olat tamid*.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai, R. Elazar and R. Yishmael: the Sinai *olah* was an *olat re'iyah*.
Beit Hillel, R. Akiva and R. Yosi HaGlili: it was an *olat tamid*.

chart.caption: What was the *olah* at Sinai? (Abaye's alignment)
rows: The *tamid* was commanded at Sinai but not offered there
Olat re'iyah (later struck from the list)
*Pratot* came only at the Ohel Mo'ed, so no *tamid* without *hefshet*
Offered at Sinai and never interrupted

children.title: Kelalot at Sinai, Peratot Later? R. Yishmael vs. R. Akiva
children.gist: R. Yishmael's view of how the Torah was given, general rules first and details later, is what places him with Beit Shammai; R. Akiva holds that both came at Sinai.

bullets.text: R. Yishmael: *kelalot ne'emru be'Sinai, u'feratot be'Ohel Mo'ed*. The general rules came at Sinai and the details later.
So a Sinai *tamid* would have been offered without *hefshet ve'nituach*, which only became required later. That seems impossible.
R. Akiva: rules and details were both given at Sinai, repeated at the Ohel Mo'ed, and taught a third time in Arvot Mo'av.
The positions seem inverted: R. Akiva derives laws from every letter, while R. Yishmael holds *dibrah Torah kilshon benei adam*.
A resolution: for R. Akiva, details "given at Sinai" means encoded in the text for the Sages to derive. For R. Yishmael, details count as given only once they are stated explicitly.

illustration.caption: R. Yishmael and R. Akiva on when the details of the mitzvot were given. For R. Yishmael, a *tamid* offered at Sinai would have come before the laws of *hefshet ve'nituach* were given.

children.title: Hefshet Ve'nituach, and When the Tamid Began
children.gist: Why R. Yishmael can't allow a changing *tamid*, and the sources for R. Elazar and R. Akiva.

bullets.text: "Is there anything that at first didn't need *hefshet ve'nituach* and later did?" Therefore, for R. Yishmael, the Sinai *olah* must have been a *re'iyah*.
Tosafot: *hefshet ve'nituach* is written in the *tamid*'s own *parashah*. So a *tamid* that changed would be especially hard to accept. A private *olah* would be less of a problem.
R. Elazar on "*olat tamid ha'asuyah be'Har Sinai*" (Bamidbar 28:6): its procedures were told at Sinai, but it wasn't offered until the Mishkan. So the Sinai *olah* was a *re'iyah*.
R. Akiva: it was offered at Sinai and never stopped.
Challenge from Amos 5:25: "Did you bring Me sacrifices... forty years in the wilderness?"
Answer: *shevet Levi*, who didn't worship the calf, offered it from their own funds, so the nation as a whole didn't.
The verse is odd on any view. Even per R. Elazar, the *tamid* ran from the second year, so thirty-nine years at least.

children.title: R. Yosi HaGlili: Olah vs. Chagigah vs. Shalmei Simchah
children.gist: Three pilgrimage offerings, each with its own unique feature. Since only the *chagigah* preceded Sinai, the Sinai *olah* must have been the *tamid*.

bullets.text: *Re'iyah*, *chagigah* and *simchah*: each has something the other two lack.
The *chagigah*'s distinction is that it existed before the *dibbur*. That is the same fact Beit Hillel rely on.
If the *re'iyah* did not precede Sinai, the *olah* in Shemot 24 was the *olat tamid*.
Open question: why call the Sinai *shelamim* a *chagigah* and not a *simchah*? The Gemara doesn't say.

chart.caption: R. Yosi HaGlili: what each pilgrimage offering has that the others lack
rows: Goes entirely to God; the other two are mostly eaten
Obligates women as well as men

children.title: R. Yishmael Struck from the List
children.gist: R. Yosi HaGlili's own *baraita* undercuts Abaye's reasoning about R. Yishmael, so the Gemara strikes R. Yishmael from the list.

bullets.text: Why put R. Yishmael with Beit Shammai? Only because of the *hefshet ve'nituach* argument.

But R. Yosi HaGlili holds that the Sinai *olah* was a *tamid* and also that it needed no *hefshet ve'nituach*, a requirement that began at the Ohel Mo'ed. So a changing *tamid* is a coherent position.
Nothing forces R. Yishmael's view, so the Gemara deletes him from Abaye's list (*u'machkeih le'Rabbi Yishmael mehakha*).
Beit Shammai's reading makes Sinai a moment of encounter (*vayechezu et ha'Elokim*). Beit Hillel's makes it the quiet, daily *tamid*: worship as steady routine.

returns_to.note: Revisits Abaye's placement of R. Yishmael

children.title: Shemot 24:5: Were the Olot Bulls Too? Teiku
children.gist: Rav Chisda: in Shemot 24:5, does "bulls" describe both offerings or only the *shelamim*? The question is left unresolved.

bullets.text: Is there a break after "*vaya'alu olot*"? Then the *olot* were sheep and only the *shelamim* were bulls. Or does "*parim*" cover both?
Mar Zutra: the practical difference is where the cantillation places its break.
Rav Acha b. Rava: one who vows "an *olah* like the one at Sinai". Must he bring a bull or a sheep?
*Teiku*: the question stands.

returns_to.note: Returns to Shemot 24:5, the verse both schools cited

sections.title: Re'iyah: No Minimum or Maximum
sections.gist: The Mishnah in Pe'ah lists mitzvot with no fixed measure, *re'ayon* among them. The discussion continues on 7a.

bullets.text: Pe'ah 1:1: "These have no measure: *pe'ah*, *bikkurim*, *re'ayon*, *gemilut chasadim* and Torah study."
Does "no measure" rule out a floor, a ceiling or both? Compare the Yerushalmi on *pe'ah*, and R. Yochanan's view that one may make a whole field *bikkurim*.

sections.continues: Continues on 7a: R. Yochanan's first reading, R. Oshaya's correction, and R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on *re'ayon*.

judgment_calls: R. Yosi HaGlili's three offerings is conceptually self-contained and could be its own top-level section; kept under the Sinai debate because the Gemara cites it as the source for his position there.
Rabbi Yishmael Realigned returns to the Positions subsection; kept in Gemara order with a returns_to link rather than moved.
Parsing the Verse could sit under the Beit Hillel / Beit Shammai reasons (it returns to their verse); kept as the last step of the Sinai debate, where it falls in the text.
coverage_notes: The minor's-obligation exchange (5b–6a) isn't discussed in this shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only.
The essay says the Gemara 'reassigns R. Yishmael to Beit Hillel'; the text only deletes him from Abaye's list. Followed the text.
The segmentation names R. Eliezer where the text has R. Elazar. Followed the text.
The shiur continues into 7a (re'iyah without a measure; R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish); outside this daf's scope.
